text:
Jacek Karpiński was born in 1927 in Turin, Italy, into a family of Polish intellectuals and alpinists. His father, Adam Karpiński, was an aeronautic engineer and inventor, while his mother, Wanda Czarnocka-Karpińska, was a physician and later Dean of the University of Physical Education in Warsaw. The family moved to Warsaw in 1934, where Karpiński's father died during an expedition to the Himalayas in 1939.
During World War II, Karpiński joined the Gray Ranks, a Polish underground paramilitary organization, and participated in numerous operations, including the Warsaw Uprising. He was severely injured during a sabotage operation and lost sight in both eyes, but recovered fully with the help of his mother. He was awarded the Cross of Valour three times for his actions.
After the war, Karpiński attended local high school, completed his curriculum in one year, and enrolled at the Faculty of Electro-Mechanical Sciences in Łódź. He later transferred to the Warsaw University of Technology, where he graduated in 1951.
Karpiński's major achievements include the development of the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) in 1957 and the AKAT-1, the world's first differential equations analyzer based on transistors, in 1959. AKAT-1 was praised for its innovative design and aesthetic appeal, with its panel designed by leading Polish artists.
In 1960, he was awarded the UNESCO scholarship for young engineers, which enabled him to travel to the United States, where he met prominent computer scientists including John Eckert, Claude Shannon, and Edward F. Moore. Upon his return, he developed the Polish perceptron, one of the first such devices in the world, and later the KAR-65, a computer capable of performing 100,000 operations per second.
In 1970, Karpiński founded the Microcomputers' Construction Plant (Zakład Budowy Mikrokomputerów) to develop the K-202, a minicomputer designed for small-scale, affordable use. Despite its technical excellence, the project faced significant challenges due to political and administrative resistance, resulting in only 30 units being produced.
Karpiński later moved to Switzerland to work on Nagra tape recorders and returned to Poland in the 1990s, serving as an advisor on computer science. He was awarded the Officer's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2009 and the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2010 posthumously.
Karpiński was also a secret informant for the Służba Bezpieczeństwa (Polish security service), collecting technological data during his time in the United States. His work and legacy are debated, with some viewing him as a visionary whose innovations were stifled by political forces, while others see him as a pioneering figure in early computer science in Poland.
